scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original C1 independent assessment draft with ten new inference, argument or transfer questions. Content requires teacher approval.

tabs.title: Applying the Critique
tabs.description: Use the ideas to judge new educational situations.

questions.q: Which concern does the writer raise about apparently positive slogans on improvement?
choices: They may shift blame onto learners when practical support is missing.
They discourage students from reflecting on unsuccessful strategies.
They imply that everyone learns best through direct criticism.
They invite schools to abandon all measures of progress.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one contrasts encouraging growth language with the risk of treating structural problems as personal failures.

questions.q: Why is the comparison between the two students not simply a story about effort?
choices: The second student is shown to be less interested in learning.
Their opportunities to turn effort into progress differ.
The first student receives a different assessment.
The text shows that good strategies are never useful.
questions.explanation: Both receive the same poor result, but their access to quiet space, time and support is unequal.

questions.q: What is lost when leisure must always produce measurable improvement?
choices: The need for learners to explain their personal goals.
The value of learning through regular school assessments.
The freedom to explore without proving immediate progress.
The possibility that students will ever improve their marks.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three values reading, discussion and experimentation even without measurable outcomes.

questions.q: Why does the author acknowledge that both students might benefit from better strategies?
choices: To suggest the second student's difficulties are mainly motivational.
To prove that the same study advice will produce equal results.
To explain why teachers should rank students by effort.
To avoid presenting support and personal agency as alternatives.
questions.explanation: The concession preserves the value of strategies while distinguishing them from the resources needed to use them.

questions.q: What is the role of the sentence about a quiet room or an extra hour?
choices: It shows that time management is the writer's primary concern.
It identifies a practical limit of otherwise sensible advice.
It suggests that all students should be given identical homework.
It explains why study plans are ineffective for every student.
questions.explanation: The example grounds the argument that advice cannot itself provide missing study conditions.

questions.q: How does the last paragraph develop rather than reject individual responsibility?
choices: It argues that students should leave most decisions to schools.
It recommends measuring the quality of every leisure activity.
It places the entire burden of improvement on teachers.
It pairs learners' decisions with institutional measures that enable them.
questions.explanation: The writer combines revising ineffective strategies with schools' obligations to provide support.

questions.q: A school praises students who improve fastest, but some students have no quiet study space. What should it examine?
choices: Whether its recognition confuses available resources with personal merit.
Whether students without space should receive no feedback.
Whether fewer assessments would always improve learning.
Whether high-scoring students should be asked to study longer.
questions.explanation: The two-student example warns that unequal access can be misread as difference in character.

questions.q: A pupil enjoys reading a novel but cannot name a measurable skill gained. What follows from the argument?
choices: The pupil should replace the novel with assessed reading.
The school should give the pupil a grade for leisure time.
The activity can still have educational value.
The experience must have been unproductive.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph maintains that valuable curiosity and exploration need not be charted.

questions.q: A teacher wants to encourage persistence without blaming students. Which approach fits the text?
choices: Display more motivational slogans without changing access.
Offer concrete support and specific feedback alongside encouragement.
Ask students to explain publicly why they have not improved.
Measure effort only by the time spent studying.
questions.explanation: The conclusion names practical support and precise feedback as ways to make agency meaningful.

questions.q: What would best demonstrate the author's preferred balance in a school policy?
choices: Students are judged by the same effort score regardless of circumstances.
Rest is rewarded only when it raises the next test result.
No outcomes are recorded because measurement is undesirable.
Students can revise their work and access supported study time.
questions.explanation: Combining support, revision and individual responsibility reflects the final paragraph.
